To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Endoglin and activins receptor-like kinase 2 heterozygous mutant mice display distinct pulmonary and hepato-portal angiogenic profiles and that anti-VEGF anti-angiogenic treatment has a distinct effect in each model.
Endoglin and activink receptor-like kinase-1 heterozygotes show distinct pulmonary and hepatal angiogenic profile and respond differently to anti-VEGFA treatment.
Endoglin and Activin receptor-like kinase-1 heterozygote mice show distinct pulmonary and hepic angiogenic profiles and response to anti VEGF therapy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the pathophysiology of HHT and the development of novel therapeutic approaches.
the mechanisms of vascular disease and the development of therapeutic strategies for the treatment of HHT and other diseases of the blood vessels.
the mechanisms of angiogenesis, and the role of the TGF-β superfamily receptors in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mechanisms responsible to the angiogenic imbalance differ between Endoglin and Activin receptor-like kinase1 heterozygote mice, and that the response to anti VEGF therapy is organ specific.

the angiogenesis phenotype in Eng (+/-)/Alk1 (+/-)/wild-type mice is different in the liver and lung, that the angiogenic defect is more pronounced in Eng (+/-), and that anti-VEGF antibody therapy has distinct effects on angiogenesis in the liver and in the lung.
the angiogenic phenotype of HHT1 and HHT2 is organ-specific and that anti-VEGF may have a therapeutic potential in HHT1 patients, but not in HHT2 patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pulmonary and hepatic vascular beds are distinct with respect to the response to antiangiogenic therapy.
the angiogenic profile of heterozygous Endoglin and Activin receptor-like kinase1 mice differs between organs and is distinct between the two mutant models.
the pulmonary angiogenic defect and RVH in Eng(+/-) mice is associated with a rise in TSP-1, which is normalized by anti-VEGFR2 treatment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
anti-VEGF may not be the most appropriate therapy to treat HHT patients and other therapies targeting the TGF-β superfamily signaling pathway may be more appropriate.
the response to antiangiogenic therapy differs between Eng and Alks mutant mice and that the mechanisms responsible are distinct between these two models of HHT.

antiangiogenic therapy may have different effects on the angiogenesis of different organs in the same animal, and therefore, should not be used as a general therapy in HHT patients, but should be targeted to the organ that needs it the most.
